title: Trade Integration, Market Size, and Industrialization: Evidence from China's National Trunk Highway System
research_question: How does the connection of small peripheral regions to large metropolitan centers via large-scale highway infrastructure affect economic growth, industrial output, and urbanization in those peripheral regions? Specifically, do reductions in trade costs between ex ante asymmetric markets diffuse industrial and total economic activity to peripheral areas, or do they reinforce the spatial concentration of production in metropolitan cores?
data_description: The study compiles a county-level panel covering 1,748 historically consistent geo-referenced Chinese county units (out of 2,341 administrative units, across 33 provinces and 349 prefectures). County-level socioeconomic data—including GDP broken into agricultural, industrial, and services gross value added, local government revenues, registered populations, urban populations, education, and sectoral employment shares—are drawn from Provincial Statistical Yearbooks for 1990, 1997, and 2006, and from the 1990 Population Census, obtained from the University of Michigan's China Data Center and the CITAS project. Geo-referenced administrative boundaries (1999) and digitized highway routes, classified by completion phase (pre-1997, 1997–2003, post-2003), come from the ACASIAN Data Center. Land cover and elevation data are from the USGS Digital Chart of the World and ACASIAN hydrology data. The unit of observation is the county, with key outcomes measured as log changes between 1997 and 2006.
institutional_context: China's National Trunk Highway System (NTHS), approved by the State Council in 1992, was a US$120 billion, ~35,000 km expressway program built largely between 1992 and 2007. Its stated objective was to connect all provincial capitals, cities with urban registered populations above 500,000, and border crossings on a single four-lane expressway network. Although the targeted metropolitan centers represented only 1.5% of land area and 17% of population, they accounted for 60% of non-agricultural production prior to construction; the average pre-existing GDP gap between non-targeted peripheral counties and targeted nodes was roughly 1:25. As a by-product of linking these major nodes, many small peripheral counties along intermediate routes were connected to large metropolitan agglomerations. Financing relied heavily on provincial and county borrowing against future toll revenues, and construction accelerated after 1998 as part of post–Asian-crisis stimulus.
